query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy multilayers, sustained loading promotes a progressive transition from homogeneous dislocation slip to localized deformation mechanisms—namely, deformation twinning and strain‐induced short-range ordering—primarily governed by the constrained nanoscale interfaces. These interfaces act as structural mediators that enhance local stress concentrations and facilitate the activation of subsidiary slip systems, thereby balancing strength with deformability.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanoscale multilayer coating composed of alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy alloy phases exhibiting inherent compositional complexity, lattice distortion, and initial short-range chemical order.
generation.intervention: Application of sustained mechanical loading (creep conditions) while systematically varying the multilayer's interfacial spacing (layer thickness) under controlled temperature conditions.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted at a fixed temperature (e.g., room temperature) under constant sub-yield stress, ensuring that the coating remains intact and that the multilayer architecture is preserved.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale interfaces between layers that concentrate stress, accentuate lattice distortions, and modify local short-range order, thus mediating the shift from uniform dislocation glide to localized twinning and ordering.
generation.mechanism: Under sustained loading, the initial plasticity via dislocation slip is progressively supplemented by deformation twinning and localized strain-induced ordering at the heterogeneous interfaces. The constrained geometry and compositional gradients augment stress concentrations that lower the energy barrier for activating twin formation, while the evolving short-range order further impedes dislocation motion, leading to a controlled, progressive plastic deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to an unstrained baseline multilayer (which deforms primarily via dislocation glide), the sustained loading will result in an increased density of deformation twins and measurable changes in local ordering near the layer interfaces. A critical interfacial dimension or stress threshold should mark the onset of this mechanistic shift.
generation.baseline: Multilayer coatings in the as-deposited state, where deformation is dominated by homogeneous dislocation activity with minimal twinning or strain-induced ordering.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to nanoscale multilayer coatings (layer thickness below ~100 nm) under moderate to high sustained loads that do not cause catastrophic failure, within the temperature range where diffusion-mediated effects are minimal.
generation.uncertainty: The precise relative contributions of twinning versus dislocation activity and the quantitative threshold stress or layer thickness at which the mechanism transition occurs remain uncertain due to limited direct experimental data in FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy multilayers.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate nanoscale multilayer coatings with alternating FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy layers of controlled thickness. Subject these samples to sustained creep tests at a constant temperature and load while using in situ TEM and diffraction techniques to monitor the evolution of dislocation structures, twin formation, and local ordering at the interfaces.
measurements: Dislocation density and morphology across interfaces (via TEM)
Twin volume fraction and distribution (via high-resolution imaging)
Changes in local short-range order (via electron diffraction or atom probe tomography)
Creep strain rate and total plastic strain over time
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If sustained loading does not result in a statistically significant increase in deformation twinning or measurable changes in local short-range order at the layer interfaces compared to the baseline homogeneous dislocation-dominated deformation, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Small-Scale Insight into Uniform Deformability and Softening Resistance of Refractory High-Entropy Alloy

Abstract: Owing to the outstanding softening resistance and thermal stability of BCC-structured refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs), their unique deformation-induced defect structures merit investigation. Therefore, this study evaluated the mechanical properties and deformation behaviors of W-based low- to high-entropy alloys at various temperatures and orientations using nanoindentation and microcompression, complemented by post-mortem TEM and atomistic simulations to observe dislocation populations and their evolution. Results reveal that HEAs exhibit reduced elastic and plastic anisotropy while retaining high-temperature strength. With increasing compositional complexity, planar slip and abrupt stress drops were progressively replaced by homogeneous flow and smoother serrations. Severe lattice distortion promoted dislocation nucleation but impeded long-range glide, enabling cooperative edge and screw dislocation activity that sustained strength and work hardening across temperatures.

Tuning superelasticity in high entropy alloy via a hidden strain order

Abstract: AbstractSuperelasticity – exhibiting either Hookean (linear) or non-Hookean (nonlinear) recoverable strain beyond 2% – has been realized in distinct material systems such as metallic glasses, shape memory alloys, strain glass alloys and Gum metals, enabling diverse technological applications. Here we demonstrate that, through compositional tuning in a high-entropy alloy, the elastic behavior can be continuously and reversibly modulated between Hookean superelasticity, non-Hookean superelasticity with an ultrahigh recoverable strain of ~8%, and back to the Hookean regime. By combining atomic-scale strain mapping and extensive first-principles calculations, we reveal that this tunability is governed by a hidden strain order, arising from frustrated crystallization of two competing phases. As a result, local lattice distortion arises, producing a heterogeneous strain landscape that modulates phase stability, phase transformation propensity, and elastic response. Dislocations and deformation microstructure in a B2-ordered Al28Co20Cr11Fe15Ni26 high-entropy alloy

Abstract: High-entropy alloys are multicomponent metallic materials currently attracting high research interest. They display a unique combination of chemical disorder and crystalline long-range order, and due to their attractive properties are promising candidates for technological application. Many high-entropy alloys possess surprisingly high strength, occasionally in combination with high ductility and low density. The mechanisms effecting these attractive mechanical properties are not understood. This study addresses the deformation mechanism of a Al28Co20Cr11Fe15Ni26 high-entropy alloy, which is a two-phase material, consisting of a B2-ordered matrix and disordered body-centred inclusions. We quantitatively analyse the microstructure and dislocations in deformed samples by transmission-electron-microscopic methods including weak-beam imaging and convergent-beam electron diffraction. Atomistic clustering-ordering and high-strain deformation of an Al0.1CrCoFeNi high-entropy alloy

Abstract: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. On the evolving nature of c/a ratio in a hexagonal close-packed epsilon martensite phase in transformative high entropy alloys

Abstract: Activation of different slip systems in hexagonal close packed (h.c.p.) metals depends primarily on the c/a ratio, which is an intrinsic property that can be altered through alloying addition. In conventional h.c.p. alloys where there is no diffusion-less phase transformation and associated transformation volume change with deformation, the c/a ratio remains constant during deformation. In the present study, c/a ratio and transformation volume change of h.c.p. epsilon martensite phase in transformative high entropy alloys (HEAs) were quantified as functions of alloy chemistry, friction stir processing and tensile deformation. The study revealed that while intrinsic c/a is dependent on alloying elements, c/a of epsilon in transformative HEAs changes with processing and deformation. This is attributed to transformation volume change induced dependence of h.c.p. lattice parameters on microstructure and stress state. Lower than ideal c/a ratio promotes non-basal pyramidal 〈c + a〉 slip and deformation twinning in epsilon phase of transformative HEAs.

Tensile deformation behavior of twist grain boundaries in CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy bicrystals

Abstract: AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEA) are a class of materials that consist of multiple elemental species in similar concentrations. The use of elements in far from dilute concentrations introduces a multi-dimensional composition design space by which the properties of metallic systems can be tailored. While the mechanical behavior of HEAs has been the subject of active research recently, the role of grain boundaries (GBs) in their deformation behavior remains poorly understood. Amorphization in extreme deformation of the CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy

Abstract: Extreme deformation of high-entropy alloys increases toughness by converting crystalline structures to amorphous zones. Ever-harsher service conditions in the future will call for materials with increasing ability to undergo deformation without sustaining damage while retaining high strength. Prime candidates for these conditions are certain high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which have extraordinary work-hardening ability and toughness. By subjecting the equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi HEA to severe plastic deformation through swaging followed by either quasi-static compression or dynamic deformation in shear, we observe a dense structure comprising stacking faults, twins, transformation from the face-centered cubic to the hexagonal close-packed structure, and, of particular note, amorphization. The Effect of Phase Separation on the Mechanical Behavior of the Co–Cr–Cu–Fe–Ni High-Entropy Alloy

Abstract: AbstractPhase separation phenomena in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted much attention since their discovery, but little attention has been given to the dynamics of the deformation mechanism of this kind of HEA during uniaxial tension, which limits their widespread and practical utility. In this work, molecular dynamics simulation was used to study the effect of phase separation on the mechanical properties of an HEA under uniaxial tensile loading. Moreover, the associated deformation behavior of the Co–Cr–Cu–Fe–Ni HEA was investigated at the nanoscale. Models with Cu-rich grain boundaries or grains were constructed. The results showed that Cu-rich grain boundaries or grains lowered the strength of the Co–Cr–Cu–Fe–Ni HEA, and Cu-rich grain boundaries significantly reduced ductility. This change of mechanical properties was closely associated with a deformation behavior. Mechanically derived short-range order and its impact on the multi-principal-element alloys

Abstract: Chemical short-range order in disordered solid solutions often emerges with specific heat treatments. Unlike thermally activated ordering, mechanically derived short-range order (MSRO) in a multi-principal-element Fe40Mn40Cr10Co10 (at%) alloy originates from tensile deformation at 77 K, and its degree/extent can be tailored by adjusting the loading rates under quasistatic conditions.
